newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Small is big on Malaysia's 2nd board.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Small is big on Malaysia's 2nd board.

text.p: It is not the steady dividend payments of a utility or the solidity of a colonial-era plantations firm that makes the blood pump here.
No, this is the realm of the small-time speculator in small-capitalisation stocks in Malaysia, where big money can be made by those daring to go where few players have gone before.
That conviction took the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's Second Board index of nearly 200 small-capitalised stocks to record highs in September.
But a correction did hit the index last week when it dropped almost four percent amid concerns over financing restrictions on buying Second Board stocks.
The cooling off probably came as a relief to market regulators, who want shorter settlement trade periods, a move that will certainly dampen speculation.
Still, business is good for the brokerage industry. At TA Securities Bhd, Malaysia's largest retail brokerage, the public gallery was a hive of activity on a recent visit.
Several dozen people sat glued to eight television-sized screens showing stock prices and graphs in multi-coloured hues.
Others clustered around their remisiers (freelance brokers) studying the ebb and flow of money on the Second Board, which can turn over as much as 200 million ringgit (US$80 million) daily.

It's a world where timber, gaming, rug making, building materials and rubber sheet firms all jostle for the fancy of retirees, young professionals and housewives with a hot tip, cool cash and a stalwart heart.
Some investors undoubtedly bone up on annual reports, brokerage house recommendations and newspaper articles.
"You've got to know what kind of stock it is, who's the owner, what's the business," said one man in his early 30s.
But speculation, rather than serious research seems to be the driving force, an issue that concerns market regulators.
"A lot of people follow other people. They will lose one day," said the man, the owner of a small insurance agency.
For some, stock market watching has become a full-time job. A woman in her 60s settles down with a home-packed lunch of rice. "Just like home," she said.

She comes in every day at 8 a.m., an hour-and-a-half before the market starts trading. "I buy a little," she added. She listens to her friends' tips and tries to get in on the often lucrative new listings.
Investors like these laugh at the idea of buying blue chip stocks from the Composite Index's 100.
"Initially, I was interested in the main board," said a 52-year-old co-owner of an electrical business. "But the main board let me down. Prices have been stagnant."
Compared to a near doubling of the Second Board index since the end of 1995, the Composite Index has risen just 13 percent in the first nine months of this year.
"In the Malaysian market there are few investors, but many speculators," said a retiree, 'Uncle Soon' to regulars.
But none of the punters said they would risk their life savings on stocks.
A remisier with seven years' experience and witness to Malaysia's 1993 bull run said he urges caution on his customers. "I don't encourage them to over-trade," he said. "Most are retired people."

The insurance agency owner said the biggest killing he ever made on a single stock was 100,000 ringgit (US$40,000). He continues to trade in ten or so stocks at any given time, although he said that three or four are easier to track.
Concerns about speculation aside, the bull run in secondary stocks has undeniably been good for many investors, remisiers and firms.

"We are fortunate to have such an active market," said Tony Tiah, founder and head of TA Securities. "Millionaires are made overnight, IPOs (Initial Public Offerings) are in demand. I think that's a very good sign."
